title: The Dichotomy of Control — rich
forward_vector: I am the manifest of The Dichotomy of Control's rich face, its first round at Sketch tier, a proposal: one made walk for the technical face, which builds the page's own situation (a plant, a disturbance, a controller with a bounded actuator) as a turntable platter and puts the page's sentence against it under rules stated before the runs. The Life Face has no piece: its claim is a practice, not a measure, and a sorting toy would only score costs I made up. I grow toward the worked example the page owes, one real decision sorted in two columns, if Loudon wants it played. I never hold the entry's words.

offers.what: 'Everything else — load, noise, the plant's own dynamics, the future reference — is disturbance' puts four things in one bin, and the platter meets them four ways. Load is disturbance, and a model of it rejects it: a memory (I) removes a steady finger's drag, and a once-a-turn model takes a rub's wow from 1.43% to 0.02% (the sensor's floor, 0.021%) at Kp 5, Ki 2. Noise is not rejected at any gain: P alone at Kp 1, 5 and 20 shakes the platter 0.020%, 0.064% and 0.34%, because the controller acts on its sensor's mistakes; the more it pushes, the more it lets in. The plant's own dynamics are not rejected either: the belt's 0.15 s lag sets the edge past which the loop swings for good (Kp 23.5, by Routh and by the run). The reference is followed, not rejected (a reading, not a piece). Suggested: 'A controller can only command its actuators. Everything else is not up to it — the load, the noise in its own measurements, the plant's dynamics, the reference it is given — and it meets each differently: it rejects a disturbance by modelling it, declines to act on noise, is designed around the plant, and follows the reference.' This is the mapping the agency profile asks for, made exact. The numbers are this model platter's, not a real turntable's.

'Not to fight' holds because of what every real loop has, and the page doesn't say so. On an ideal platter (no belt lag, no sensor noise) fighting costs nothing: Kp 100, Ki 40 brings the rub's wow to 0.05% with no jitter. On the real one, fighting at Kp 20, Ki 8 leaves 0.34% wow, adds 0.41% jitter and moves the motor three times as much (0.214 against 0.065) as the model that leaves 0.02%. And a model rejects only what it is a model of: tuned to 0.40 Hz instead of once a turn (0.556 Hz) it leaves 1.70% wow, worse than no model (1.43%). Suggested, after 'not to fight': 'Fighting — turning the gain up to answer every error harder — feeds the loop's own noise and lag back into what it controls, and a model rejects only the disturbance it is a model of.' The last clause is the Serenity Prayer's third line in control terms: the wisdom to know the difference is the model.

The blurred middle, measured once. A hand pressing at 0.9 of a motor's full torque, when holding speed needs 1.3, is partly within reach and partly not: the seam runs through the hand, not between things. The motor gives all it has (pinned from about 4.1 s), and four times the gain (asking 16.9 against 65.5) ends the press at the same 25.4%, where the platter's own balance says it must: (1 − 0.9) ÷ 0.4 = 25%. What costs is holding on. A memory that keeps adding up the error it can't act on overshoots 129% when the hand lifts; one that holds still at the limit (anti-windup), 6.4%. Offered as one answer to the first question, not as Loudon's reading: 'In a controller the middle needs no third column. The seam runs through the thing, at the actuator's limit; act up to it, and what costs is the memory that keeps pushing past it.' Found by the piece's step 6; the null (a hand the motor holds without reaching its limit) shows the release changes nothing there.

pieces.title: The hand on the platter · authority, disturbance and the grip
pieces.caption:
**Does a controller do best by spending effort only where it has authority, and modelling the rest instead of fighting it?** Seven steps on a turntable platter. First the platter alone: the motor is yours to set, a finger on the edge is not, and it slows to half speed. Then a controller that pushes back, on an ideal platter, where fighting harder simply works: the sag is 0.2 ÷ (0.4 + Kp). Then the belt's lag and the sensor's noise every real loop has: now more gain shakes the platter with the sensor's mistakes, and past Kp 23.5 it swings for good. Then a memory, which removes a steady drag at a modest gain. Then a rub that comes round once a turn: fighting it at Kp 20 leaves 0.34% wow and adds 0.41% jitter; a once-a-turn model at Kp 5 leaves 0.02%, the sensor's floor; the model tuned wrong leaves 1.70%, worse than none. Then a hand heavier than the motor can hold: four times the gain ends the press at the same 25.4%, and a memory that keeps winding overshoots 129% when the hand lifts, against 6.4% for one that lets go. Last, the page's sentence against fourteen runs, under four rules stated before them. The model's limits: a round-number platter, a linear belt and sensor, a rub of one pure frequency, and noise of one size. Its percentages are its own, not a real turntable's. *Hear it* plays 33⅓ as 440 Hz beside the platter's own tone: a sag is a beat, wow a beat that comes and goes once a turn.
